A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MuLoCo and retain the same core optimization framework. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable. Changed experimental settings and internal reporting inconsistencies limit particular performance interpretations but do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model pretraining experiments comparing MuLoCo, DiLoCo, data-parallel baselines and compression methods, including additional experiments in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 reports original pretraining experiments from 150M to 15B parameters, pseudogradient analyses, downstream benchmark evaluations and system measurements in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The Muon inner optimizer, Nesterov outer optimizer and optional error-feedback rule remain. v2 adds a streaming adaptation with staggered updates across three parameter partitions and explicitly incorporates two quantizations into compressed communication (Section 6.4; Appendix C.1). These extend communication handling while retaining the core optimizer.

E1.justification: Pretraining changes from FineWeb-EDU to high-quality Nemotron-CC. v2 also adds zero-shot evaluation on MMLU, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, ARC-E, ARC-C and OBQA (Tables 3 and 8), substantially extending v1's pretraining-loss evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: The principal optimizer comparators remain DiLoCo, data-parallel AdamW and data-parallel Muon. v2 additionally evaluates Streaming DiLoCo and distinguishes global/row-wise linear and statistical quantizer comparisons. v1's DCT Top-k and Random-k comparisons disappear (v1 Appendix C; v2 Figures 8 and 15).

E3.justification: v1's single roughly 220M model, GPT-2 tokenizer, 512-token context and 3.6B-token budget are replaced by Gemma3-style models, Llama3 tokenization, 2048-token contexts and a 150M–15B scaling study. v2 sweeps worker counts, synchronization intervals, batch sizes and additional optimizer hyperparameters, introduces new evaluation procedures, and extrapolates rather than fully tunes 15B settings (Sections 5–7; Appendices E–F).

E4.justification: Beyond v1's compression and error-feedback ablations, v2 adds controlled pseudogradient alignment, spectral interference and step-norm analyses; worker-count and synchronization sensitivity; streaming tests; critical-batch-size studies; and scaling-law sensitivity analyses. Appendices C, D and F add supporting diagnostics. The earlier DCT and Random-k analyses are removed.

E5.justification: v2 introduces a time-weighted EMA final-loss estimator (Appendix F), robust log-space Huber scaling-law estimation with 512 fitting restarts (Section 7.1), and median system timings over 500 steps. These substantially expand statistical estimation beyond v1. Fitting restarts are not repeated training runs; neither version reports training-seed confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v1's near-lossless 2-bit MuLoCo result with error feedback gives way to quantizer-dependent findings under v2's changed setup, including degradation with global linear quantization. Numerous scaling, diagnostic, timing and downstream results are added: Table 8 reports 3.1B mean accuracy of 57.65% for MuLoCo K=1 versus 56.79% for DiLoCo K=1. v2's Tables 3 and 7 disagree on 15B loss rankings, limiting precise interpretation.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the formal interference-gap definition, Proposition 4.2 relating pseudogradient nuclear norm to step alignment and magnitude, Muon/AdamW corollaries, and an Appendix B proof. This adds substantial mathematical analysis beyond v1's algorithm and background, including assumptions about orthonormal updates and negligible weight decay.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion shift from compression and the 2-bit/8-fold communication headline to improved worker scaling, larger critical batch sizes, single-worker performance–time efficiency, and scalability to 15B. v2 also makes pseudogradient structure and its theoretical explanation central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds spectral interference and step-alignment explanations for worker scaling, while explicitly acknowledging that the evidence does not establish causality. It qualifies error-feedback usefulness by quantization regime and discusses dense-transformer/20-token-per-parameter scope, extrapolation uncertainty, incomplete 15B tuning, and assumptions behind idealized timing comparisons.

D1.justification: v1's Optax implementation description is replaced by distributed Muon and fused PyTorch implementations using TorchTitan/TorchFT. v2 adds a project code link, H100/H200 and distributed-training details, extensive per-scale hyperparameter tables, fitting procedures and evaluation-loss instructions. However, v1's explicit error-feedback beta selections are no longer provided.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around single-worker optimization, discussing Lookahead, Reptile, SNOO and GPA, and adds SparseLoCo and extensive large-batch/scaling-law literature. These new relationships and novelty claims go beyond relocating v1's communication-focused related work from Appendix D into the main text.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, method narrative and conclusion. It moves related work into the main text, reorganizes results into communication and scaling studies, and introduces explicit findings, a limitations section and an appendix contents page. This is a broad narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: The two-column main paper becomes a largely single-column report with a redesigned title panel. The opening figure is replaced, algorithm presentation is split, and substantial diagnostic, scaling, batch-size and systems displays are added. Some panels are redisplayed rather than new evidence, notably across Figures 1/6 and 7/15.

improvement.justification: v1's practicality claim rested on one small-model study without wall-clock accounting. v2 substantially strengthens its support through tuned worker/batch-size studies, downstream evaluations up to 15B, measured optimizer overhead and fuller reproducibility information. These gains outweigh reporting problems, including unexplained 15B loss disagreements between Tables 3 and 7 and quantization discrepancies between Figure 7 and Table 5. Those inconsistencies still weaken precise numerical claims, and the bandwidth-dependent training times remain idealized estimates.
